body:
Loading... 
   Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined and several races are still outstanding.   A few in California are being contested by two candidates in the same party. So it's clear which party will hold the seat, even if it's not clear who will win. Others are too close to call or there aren't enough ballots counted to know which candidate will prevail. In many places in the country, it takes a while to count votes. That's normal and expected.   Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called in the House by The Associated Press:   
    Loading... 
   In the Senate, there are two races outstanding, Alaska and Mississippi. Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting and no candidate in the four-person race has achieved a 50% majority in the count, it may proceed to another round of counting later this month. Mississippi uses a more traditional electoral system but a large number of provisional ballots — called affidavit ballots in the state — are taking time to count. Less than 2,000 votes separate the top two candidates in that race.     Loading...

title: Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
description: A close up of the hands of a nurse from
body:
A close up of the hands of a nurse from the French Blood Establishment checking the identification and traceability of blood samples beside a donor during a mobile blood donation session in Paimpol Cotes d Armor Brittany France on July 23, 2026.
                
                    Helene Rigny/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Helene Rigny/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank.   "This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps.   
   Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage.   However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable.   "This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life."   On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation.   
   The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."   "Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said.   
   Iran, Russia and the search for the culprits   The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples.   It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups.   Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit.   Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims.   Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne.   
   "Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR.   "It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued.   Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways.   For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure.   Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss.   
   While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there.   Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model.   Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks.   Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign.   
   "Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse."   Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents.   The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy.   Weiss of Health ISAC tells NPR there are basic steps the healthcare industry can take to prevent being a victim of these opportunistic attacks.   That process "begins" by "eliminating public internet exposure," wrote Weiss, then "enforcing strict network segmentation" in order to isolate refrigeration systems "from standard enterprise and guest networks" and finally adding on safeguards "that software overrides cannot bypass" like "hard-wired mechanical cutoffs" and "independent thermal alarms."   In the Health ISAC alert, the industry is urged to separate not just refrigeration controllers from hospital IT systems, but also medical gas monitors, for one, and train staff onsite on how to take physical manual control of machines in an emergency.   Finally, the alert urges hospitals to have offline backups of their systems.   Store managers on the frontlines   Sharing intelligence about these kinds of cyberattacks can help other potential victims avoid disaster.   While Estonian grocery stores were targeted in the most recent wave of attacks, many of those store managers were on high alert thanks to warnings issued by Estonia's Information Systems Authority, RIA. "When one Selver store was attacked on 2 November, the attackers managed to change the refrigeration system's temperature setting to +50°C. However, the service provider reacted quickly and prevented significant damage," said Annika Müür, a spokesperson for RIA. "So while we can't say that Estonia managed to prevent the attacks entirely, I think this case is a good example of the importance of monitoring threats internationally, acting on early warnings and working closely with businesses to minimise the impact."   
   Weiss of Health ISAC also urged companies across sectors that are being targeted by this recent wave of attacks to share information to help others defend themselves.   "The attack highlights why timely, trusted information sharing across borders and sectors is our strongest collective defense," he wrote.   "Rapid intelligence sharing allows hospitals and health facilities globally to recognize emerging attack patterns, verify vendor exposure, and harden critical infrastructure before threat actors can cause physical harm."

title: Voters under 30 helped drive Tuesday's blue wave
description: Young voters played a large role in Democratic wins in this week's midterms. People under 30 voted blue at much higher rates than in 2024.
body:
Young voters played a large role in Democratic wins in this week's midterms. People under 30 voted blue at much higher rates than in 2024.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  One of the many groups that swung back toward Democrats this week were young voters. They were long seen as part of the Democratic base, but voters under 30 shifted right two years ago, motivated by Donald Trump's pledge to better their economic prospects. So what caused them to so decisively shift back to Democrats? NPR political reporter Elena Moore has been looking into the results. Elena, so we know about the blue wave, pretty clear this week. How big was that Gen Z blue wave?ELENA MOORE, BYLINE: Yeah. Well, you know, in recent elections, A, Democrats have done well when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried the group by nearly 50 points, according to exit polls - the largest margin Democrats have had with young people in decades. And though young voters do turn out at lower rates than older voters do, that sizable support made a difference on the margins. I mean, take a look at the Texas Senate race, for example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points. Looking at just Gen Z, voters under 30, he won it by 60 points. And, you know, other winning Democrats also won large shares of the youth vote, like in Georgia, where Jon Ossoff won 85%, and even in Kansas, where Adam Hamilton got 82%.MARTÍNEZ: Yeah, so a really big change from 2024. Any idea why?MOORE: Yeah. I mean, it's massive, like, 37-point shift to the left massive. And as for why, I mean, it's likely a mix of things. There's no denying that many young people are unhappy with Trump and his agenda. Economic issues were the top concern, and voters expressed deep frustration with the state of things. Exit polling found that more than 8 in 10 saw Trump's tariff policies as hurting the economy, and a similar share said the U.S. made the wrong decision in going to war with Iran. It's also just not a monolithic group. And another reason for the shift might once again, A, fall to young men. Trump narrowly won the group two years ago. On Tuesday, they shifted left by double digits.MARTÍNEZ: You're talking about how many young people saw their vote as a rejection of President Trump, but how much of that was driven by former Trump voters?MOORE: Yeah, yeah. I mean, I'm curious about the same thing. We don't have a ton of data on nonvoters right now. Some folks may very well have stayed home, but what we do know right now is that at least some did flip and cast ballots for Democrats this year. It's estimated that some 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this cycle. That's according to new data from CIRCLE, a nonpartisan research group at Tufts University. On a call with reporters Thursday, Leela Strong, who heads CIRCLE, gave this takeaway.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)LEELA STRONG: Young people are not transactional voters. They are acting on concerns about the economy and a democracy that isn't working for their generation, and rewarding candidates who hear and see them.MARTÍNEZ: Right. So that's that - young voters back to being a solid part of the Democratic Party base.MOORE: Not so fast, A. I mean, you know, for one, it's a generation where a plurality identify as independents. And, you know, there are high stakes for both parties right now. Young people are looking for Democrats to actually deliver the economic change they campaigned on, something that will be key if the party wants Gen Z to stay in its camp. And Republicans, on the other hand, are going to have to do a lot of work if they want to chip away at Democrats' expanded edge here. Another thing to keep in mind is this is a growing group. By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate. So investments here matter.MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's NPR political reporter Elena Moore. Elena, thanks.MOORE: Thank you.

title: Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as Trump's chief of staff
description: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles (
body:
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles (R) waves while walking to board Air Force One with White House communications aide Danielle Alvarez (L) and White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller on October 23, 2026 at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland.
                
                    Alex Wong/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Wong/Getty Images
    

   
   White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is being replaced by Stephen Miller, President Trump said Friday.   The change comes after Republicans were swept out of power during this week's midterm elections and marks a defiant note from Trump. Miller has been the architect of many of Trump's most controversial policies, dating back to his first term, particularly on immigration. Data show voters this week supported Democrats in part because of Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement.   "Stephen's been with me since the beginning. He gets it," Trump told reporters later in the afternoon.   The president said in a post on his platform Truth Social that Wiles - who was the nation's first female White House chief of staff - would continue to work for him on political operations.     
   "I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," Wiles said in a statement on X, the social media site. "While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will."   Miller currently serves as deputy chief of staff in the White House, as well as an advisor to the Department of Homeland Security, and will take over on Monday.   Wiles worked with the Trump 2020 campaign in Florida and has served as chief of staff in this White House from day one. She built a reputation as a strict manager who has reduced the staff turnover and volatility of press leaks which plagued Trump's first term in the White House.   Wiles has not given many media interviews herself, but said in a profile for Vanity Fair magazine last year, that Trump "has an alcoholic's personality," but that she was accustomed to dealing with such temperaments. "I make a speciality of it," she told the journalist Chris Whipple.     She was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year, but it was announced she was cancer free this fall.   
   Miller has been a fixture in Trump's circles since 2016 with a focus on immigration but has also been involved advising military operations in the Middle East.   In his new role, he is likely to exercise even greater influence over the president's time and attention.    The speechwriter and advisor is known for his rhetorical pugnacity and frequently appears behind Trump in the Oval Office during media events.   Miller has been unapologetic for some of the administration's most controversial actions, particularly aggressive anti-immigration crackdowns that have been popular with Trump's core voting base.     Democratic leaders on Capitol Hill disparaged the move.   House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries - widely expected to become the new House speaker - said: "Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today."   And Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer added: "Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn't have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way."   The chief of staff is a "very important gatekeeper of the president's time, and of their information and the people that are going in to see the president," said David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron who studies the role of the chief of staff.    "One of the things that they're supposed to do is kind of be a neutral broker to make sure all the voices get heard. Oftentimes, though, the chief of staff is the last person talking to the president," said Cohen.

title: No one knows how many ballots are outstanding in Mississippi's Senate race
body:
Two Madison County election commissioners inspect an affidavit ballot envelope on Thursday in Canton, Miss. The state's razor-thin U.S. Senate race is shining a spotlight on Mississippi's election processes.
                
                    Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images
    

   
   In Mississippi's too-close-to-call U.S. Senate race, every ballot matters.   But no one can say for sure how many ballots there are left to count.   The razor-thin margin between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom is shining a light on an election process in Mississippi that is among the slowest and most decentralized in the country.   "Mississippi is not a model of election administration," said Michael Morse, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who studies voting.   As of midday Friday, fewer than 2,000 votes separated the two Senate candidates. But information about exactly how many ballots were outstanding was hard to come by.   
    Loading... 
   The Colom campaign said late Tuesday it was aware of more than 15,000 provisional ballots, which require verification before they're counted. And the chair of the state Republican Party said Thursday he thought there were 20,000 outstanding ballots, including potential absentee votes that can legally be received by officials until Nov. 10 if they were postmarked by Election Day.   Mississippi's top voting official, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson, said counties run their own elections, and even his office didn't know how many provisionals were left to count. He said midday Friday over 9,000 of them had been processed.   "Until we have the certified results, the individual counties will be the best source of the latest and most up-to-date information," Watson said in a statement. There are 82 counties in Mississippi, and they are not required to transmit election results to the state until next week.   Morse said he was shocked by the lack of good information available for such a high-profile race.   "Right now I would love to know a lot of things about the process and I am struggling to figure out what is unfolding here," Morse said. "I cannot tell you basic things."   Mississippi has a relatively high rate of provisional ballots   What is becoming clear is that the rate of provisional ballots, which are called affidavit ballots in Mississippi, may end up being among the highest in the country this election cycle. Those ballots are cast by people whose eligibility is questionable, according to local officials, so those votes are segregated and officials decide on a case-by-case basis whether they will be counted.   
   If the Colom campaign's estimate of 15,000 affidavit ballots holds true, that would represent roughly 1.5% of the total ballots cast in the Senate race, according to unofficial results.   In the last midterm year, 2022, just four states had a provisional ballot rate higher than that, according to federal data. And Mississippi looks to have a provisional rate close to double of that in North Carolina this year, based on the preliminary data in both states.   
   One potential reason is an in-the-weeds detail on how Mississippi does voter registration.   In most states, when voters don't cast ballots over a certain number of election cycles, or local officials come across data that indicates a voter has moved or is ineligible for some other reason, they move that voter to what's known as "inactive" status. But the voter is still able to vote normally for a period of a few years, mandated by federal law, before they either confirm their eligibility or are eventually removed.   Mississippi is one of the few states that makes those "inactive" voters have to vote provisionally. That means those voters need to fill out another form and their information needs to be reviewed after the fact by local officials before their votes are counted.   It's unclear at this point why so many voters had questionable eligibility when they showed up to vote, although the local outlet Mississippi Today has reported extensively on the state's experimental use of credit data to cull voter lists.   Morse said that list maintenance technique is garnering attention, but it's not the whole story.   "It's pairing the experiment with credit data, which could introduce some unreliability, with an undermining of the typical procedural process [in many other states], where a voter [marked "inactive"] could cast a regular ballot for at least the next two federal general elections," Morse said.   
   Watson, the Republican secretary of state, has already come out in defense of the state's registration process.   "The extra few minutes it may take to vote via affidavit ballot are well worth the election integrity added by having cleaner voter rolls!" Watson wrote Tuesday in a post on X.   But Kathy Boockvar, the former Democratic secretary of state of Pennsylvania, told NPR that while many people who have to vote with a provisional ballot are likely to be ultimately deemed eligible, the process doesn't breed trust from those who have to interact with it.   "It feels like you have to go talk to the teacher or something in the back room," Boockvar said. "It's a little bit of a suspicious-seeming thing because somebody who's going through it generally thinks that they're eligible to vote and feels like they're being asked to do something other than that."   Boockvar added that the fact that information has been so hard to come by is a sign Mississippi hasn't been in the limelight like traditional battleground states before.   "We all have to be prepared whether we expect it or not," Boockvar said. "Transparency and good data is one of the best solutions we have to combating all the suspicion and distrust."

title: 'He's got to go': Hakeem Jeffries calls for Hegseth's removal but stops short of impeachment
description: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D
body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., at a news conference in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
    

   
   House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat who is poised to become the next Speaker of the House, says his party will push to end the war in Iran and hold Trump administration officials accountable after its midterm victories. But how far Democrats will go remains unclear.   
   Speaking with Morning Edition on Friday, Jeffries called the conflict a "war of choice" that "has skyrocketed gas prices, diesel prices and fertilizer prices," raising the cost of everyday goods.   He said Democrats "shouldn't have to wait" for the new Congress to act.    But with majorities in both chambers, Jeffries said Democrats could pass a war powers resolution to try and force President Trump to end the war. If passed, it would present President Trump with the choice to either sign or veto it. Overriding a veto would require two-thirds majorities in both chambers. As of now, Democrats are short of a veto-proof majority in both chambers.   
   Jeffries stopped short of supporting impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.   Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky has threatened to force a House vote on eight articles of impeachment unless Hegseth resigns.   "We'll have that conversation," Jeffries said, calling Hegseth "the most unqualified secretary of defense in American history."   Asked directly whether Hegseth should be impeached, Jeffries said, "I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus."   "He's got to go," he added.   Jeffries said the House Judiciary and Oversight committees would investigate alleged wrongdoing by the Trump administration.   Asked about voters calling for new Democratic leadership, including the next House speaker, Jeffries said the decision rests with the House Democratic Caucus. He defended Democrats' record, saying they had "battled Trump on every issue up until this point and then just decisively defeated him a few days ago."   Listen to the full interview using the blue button above, or read the transcript below, lightly edited for length and clarity.   Leila Fadel: The person expected to be the next House Speaker and its first Black Speaker is the current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and he joins me now to talk about what that will look like. So your party has a real mandate here in Congress, and it comes with expectations from voters that you'll make life more affordable. What is at the top of your agenda if you're elected House Speaker?   House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries: Well, it was a tremendous victory for the American people and a strong rebuke of MAGA extremism, which has made life more expensive for everyday Americans. Despite their promises to lower the high cost of living on day one. There are several steps that we can take to create a more comfortable way of life for the American people, including ending the war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed gas prices, diesel prices, and fertilizer prices, and as a result, increased the cost of groceries and everyday goods on the American people.   
   Leila Fadel: How will you know?   Jeffries: Well, we shouldn't have to wait till the new Congress until that happens. The American people have clearly spoken. Even the Vice President has expressed an understanding that it's time to end the war, or Republicans will continue to pay electoral consequences in that regard, but in the majority, having both the House and the Senate, we can advance strong war powers resolutions that the president will have to take up, get it to his desk, and then explain himself to the American people if, in fact, he decides to use his veto pen.   Fadel: Do you think he'll be willing to work with you on this? I mean, he's given some mixed messages, saying I'm ready to work with the Democrats, but I'll also be "Mr. Veto."   Jeffries: I think it's incredibly important, and that we all listen to what has been expressed by the American people throughout this campaign. We promised that we were going to relentlessly fight for a more affordable America, work to drive down the high price of groceries and gas and housing, fight to make health care affordable for every single American, and at the same period of time hold the crooks accountable for all of the corruption that has been visited upon the American people. And there's an economic cost to corruption that clearly the American people have concluded Republicans have visited upon them. So hopefully, all of my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, as a result of the roaring voices of the American people, will conclude that we should decisively act to make the lives of the American people affordable.   Fadel: I want to ask about a pressing matter. Republican Congressman and Trump critic Thomas Massie of Kentucky says he'll force a vote on the House floor of eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth if he does not resign. Here's what Hegseth said in response in a video posted online:   "You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me".    Will you and other Democrats vote to impeach if this happens?   Jeffries: We'll have that conversation. We'll have that conversation when we gather as a caucus immediately upon our return, but I've been very clear about my position with respect to Pete Hegseth. He's the most unqualified Secretary of Defense in American history. He should never have been confirmed by Senate Republicans, and we've seen all the damage that he's visited upon the American people, the world, and the Pentagon in terms of military readiness, and so I first called for Pete Hegseth to be fired by Donald Trump in the spring of 2025. I have not changed my position, and he should have resigned or been fired a long time ago. But certainly in the immediate aftermath of the stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism that the American people visited at the polls a few days ago,   
   Fadel: But is this the way? Should he be impeached?   Jeffries: Well, as I indicated, we'll have that conversation as a caucus together, and I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus, but I've been very strong and clear in my opinions as it relates to Pete Hegseth. He's got to go.   Fadel: You said yesterday that Americans don't want Democrats to get even; they want you to get things done on their behalf, specifically around affordability. Now, Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming Oversight Committee Chair, struck a very different tone. He posted online, "Lawyer up," and laid out a plan that included investigating the Trump family for possible crimes in the next Congress. Are you on the same page when it comes to accountability?   Jeffries: Yeah. Well, we've repeatedly made clear over the last two years is that we've got to relentlessly make life more affordable for the American people, while at the same period of time, visit accountability on those who have been engaged in law breaking, norm breaking, and unleashing unprecedented corruption on the American people. And so, it's my expectation, and we're working closely, of course, with Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee and Democrats on the Oversight Committee, who will lead our accountability efforts, along with all of the relevant committees across the Congress, because the levels of corruption have been unprecedented, and we've made clear to the American people that if you have folks out there who have been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people, or screwing over the American people, we're going to hold the crooks accountable. We're going to function like a separate and co-equal branch of government, as opposed to, unfortunately, what my Republican colleagues have done is to bury their heads in the sand and be nothing more than a reckless rubber stamp for Donald Trump's extreme agenda. So we got to follow the facts. We got to apply the law. We got to be guided by the Constitution, and we have to deliver a government of the people, by the people, and for the people.   
   Fadel: Now, your party had a historic win this week, but we were out across the country speaking to people, and at the same time as choosing your candidates, voters were expressing dissatisfaction with the party leadership, and what they saw as an inability to stand up to Trump meaningfully. In the last two years, they wanted new blood in the party. They said they want completely new leadership of the party. That includes for a future speaker of the House. What do you say to the voters who are skeptical of Democratic establishment leaders like yourself?   Jeffries: Well, we're going to put it into the hands of the House Democratic Caucus as we chart a path forward. But we've battled Trump on every issue up until this point, and then just decisively defeated him a few days ago.   The digital version was edited by Treye Green and Jason Breslow.

title: The incoming class of U.S. senators is full of historic firsts
description: Josh Turek, Peggy Flanagan, and Dr. Abdu
body:
Josh Turek, Peggy Flanagan, and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed are among several Democratic Senators-elect who made history on Election Day 2026.
                
                    Scott Olson/Getty Images; Dymanh Chhoun/Sahan Journal/CatchLight via Getty Images; Sylvia Jarrus for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Scott Olson/Getty Images; Dymanh Chhoun/Sahan Journal/CatchLight via Getty Images; Sylvia Jarrus for NPR
    

   
   When the newest class of U.S. senators are sworn into office in January, it will include some of America's firsts.   
   The 2026 midterm election resulted in a significant shift in the landscape of Congress as Democrats won in a big way up and down the ballot. While not all the races have been called, Democrats have flipped more than 40 House seats and picked up 7 Senate seats, giving them control of both chambers of Congress.   Here are some of the new faces to expect in the Senate who made history on Election Day.   Josh Turek of Iowa    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Josh Turek speaks during an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa.
                
                    Ellen Schmidt/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ellen Schmidt/AP
    

   
   Turek will be the first Paralympian to serve in the Senate. The Democrat is a two-time gold medalist in wheelchair basketball. Turek is paraplegic and uses a wheelchair due to spina bifida. He beat Republican Ashley Hinson in the general election.   
   Julia Letlow of Louisiana    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Julia Letlow speaks to media during an election night watch party on May 16, 2026, in Baton Rouge, La.
                
                    Matthew Hinton/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Matthew Hinton/AP
    

   
   Letlow has now made history twice. She was the first Republican woman elected to the U.S. House from Louisiana in 2021. Letlow ran for the House in a special election to replace her late husband, Congressman Luke Letlow, who died of COVID-19 in 2020. Now, Louisiana voters have decided to send her to the Senate, where she will be the first Republican woman from the state to serve. She will succeed Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, who Letlow beat in the primary election.   Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Dr. Abdul El-Sayed visits a polling precinct on the campus of the University of Michigan on November 3, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Mich.
                
                    Salwan Georges/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Salwan Georges/Getty Images
    

   
   The incoming Democratic senator is the son of Egyptian immigrants and is the first Muslim person elected to the upper chamber. El-Sayed is an epidemiologist and the former health director for the city of Detroit. He beat Republican Mike Rogers for the hotly contested seat.   Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Peggy Flanagan walks with her husband as they arrive to vote at a polling location on Election Day in St. Louis Park, Minn. on November 3, 2026.
                
                    Tim Evans/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tim Evans/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Minnesota's Democratic Lt. Governor is the first Native American elected to the Senate. Flanagan is a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe. She also made political history more than once. She was also the first woman of color elected to state office in Minnesota. Flanagan will replace outgoing Democratic Sen. Tina Smith.   Chris Pappas of New Hampshire    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Chris Pappas walks onstage to deliver his acceptance speech at a watch party at the Puritan Backroom on November 3, 2026 in Manchester, New Hampshire.
                
                    Joseph Prezioso/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Joseph Prezioso/Getty Images
    

   
   Pappas is the first openly gay man elected to the Senate and is also the first gay man to represent the state of New Hampshire. He served four terms in the House and beat Republican John Sununu in the election.   
   Annie Andrews of South Carolina    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Dr. Annie Andrews takes the stage at an election night event in Charleston, S.C. on November 3, 2026.
                
                    Mic Smith/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mic Smith/AP
    

   
   In one of the biggest election night upsets, Andrews pulled out an underdog win in deep red South Carolina. Andrews is the first woman elected to the U.S. senate from the Palmetto State. She beat Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham.   Texas and Kansas elect Democratic senators    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Democratic candidates James Talarico and Adam Hamilton won their Senate races in Texas and Kansas, respectively.
                
                    Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images; Charlie Riedel/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images; Charlie Riedel/AP
    

   
   Both states are reliably Republican and both states are sending pastors to Washington. This midterm election voters broke with the status quo and elected Democrats to represent them in the Senate.   In Texas, voters selected Democrat James Talarico as their next senator. It is the first time the Longhorn State has sent a Democrat to the chamber since 1988. Talarico won against Republican nominee Ken Paxton.   After nearly 100 years, Kansas elected a democratic senator to the chamber. Adam Hamilton will be the first Democrat that has served the state since 1932. He fended off a tough race with incumbent Republican Roger Marshall.

title: Judge halts construction of Trump's arch. And, Labor Department to release jobs report
description: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for
body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Rising prices and stagnant wages fueled frustration during this week's midterm elections, prompting voters to express their discontent at the ballot box. Similarly, the stock market experienced a downturn yesterday. Concerns about a Democratic Congress regulating AI led to a more than 5% drop in the tech-heavy Nasdaq, wiping out more than $2 trillion in market value. This decline followed from Wednesday when shares rose as investors were relieved that the midterms had made Congress's fate clear. In contrast, there has been less volatility in the job market, and today the Labor Department is set to release the latest jobs report.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Stocks sank as investors fear an incoming Democratic Congress — and states across the country — could crack down on the AI industry and data centers.
                
                    TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
    

   
   🎧 Today's jobs report is expected to show that employers added about 60,000 jobs last month, NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First. While this isn't robust growth, it should keep the unemployment rate low. As long as the job market stays stable, the Federal Reserve can focus on fighting stubbornly high inflation, which likely drove the recent election outcomes.   A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of President Trump's 250-foot arch in the capital. District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order just before midnight Friday, halting work for 14 days at the request of D.C. and Virginia governments. In her 33-page opinion, she scrutinized the administration's justifications for the arch, particularly its focus on national security and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The arch is planned for Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.   
   🎧 The judges' decision followed a contentious meeting last night, during which the National Capital Planning Commission, filled with Trump allies, voted to approve the arch, NPR's Rachel Treisman says. The commission's approval came despite significant opposition to the arch from dozens and dozens of people. After nearly nine hours, the panel gave the go-ahead, which would have allowed excavation to begin. Several Democratic lawmakers are already talking about blocking the arch. Democrat Jared Huffman of California, likely to become head of the House Natural Resources Committee, warned commissioners at yesterday's meeting that anyone advancing projects not authorized by Congress risks legal repercussions.   School enrollment is set to plunge by another 2 million kids by 2030, and education experts say the crisis will be worsened by the deportation of immigrant families with school-age children. Even before the Trump administration's policy changes, public schools faced a significant decline due to shrinking family sizes. U.S. Census data show the number of children under 18 nationwide had fallen by about 2.1 million since 2010. The Trump administration's large-scale deportations began after public schools started facing a demographic crisis, with a Migration Policy Institute study indicating that 1.9 million people left the U.S. during Trump's second term. This situation marks the first time in nearly a century that birth rates and immigration levels are both low at the same time.   
   Harmeet Dhillon has left her position as head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division after 18 tumultuous months. During her time in the role, she transformed the unit, saw a significant loss of career staff and aggressively pursued Trump's agenda. She is the first senior official to depart since Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterms. Dhillon called the role "the honor of a lifetime."   Healthy or hype?   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Father and son holding toothbrushes and toothpaste in a bathroom, sharing a relaxed morning oral care routine together.
                
                    mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images
    

   
   Healthy or Hype? is an NPR series helping readers and listeners sort truth from fiction when it comes to online health claims.   Many people are replacing their fluoride dental products with those containing hydroxyapatite. It is a mineral that boasts cavity protection, whitening and enamel strengthening — all without fluoride. While health experts widely agree that fluoride is beneficial to health, interest in fluoride-free alternatives is growing. A driving force behind the trend is Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. blaming water fluoridation for health issues like arthritis, bone fractures, bone cancer and neurodevelopmental disorders. Here's what dentists say about it.   🪥 Fluoride has been extensively researched, especially in long-term studies, but early research on hydroxyapatite shows promising results.🪥 For patients considering both options, Bennett Amaechi, a professor of dentistry at the University of Texas at San Antonio, recommends using fluoride because there is more evidence supporting its effectiveness.🪥 Amaechi was an author of a 2021 study in Scientific Reports that followed 177 children for a year and compared hydroxyapatite and fluoride toothpaste. The findings showed similar outcomes of tooth decay in both groups.🪥 The American Dental Association told NPR that it acknowledges that more people are using hydroxyapatite products, which may aid in remineralization. However, they noted that research on its clinical effectiveness is still limited and unclear.🪥 The ADA recommends brushing teeth twice daily for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, flossing every day and visiting a dentist regularly.   
   Weekend picks   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                James Spader as Ultron and Paul Bettany as Vision in VisionQuest.
                
                    Marvel
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Marvel
    

   
   Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:   🍿 Movies: John Turturro stars as Harry, a skilled pickpocket and caretaker for his wife, in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York. His life changes dramatically when he steals a backpack from a college kid, only to discover he is the grandson of a crime boss.   📺 TV: VisionQuest is Marvel's finale series to the trilogy that started with WandaVision and continued through Agatha All Along. It serves as a timely parable about artificial intelligence, while also exploring themes of daddy issues, according to Pop Culture Happy Hour.   📚 Books: As it gets cooler, it's the perfect time to cozy up with a good book. Here are six must-read November releases, featuring tales of star-crossed romance, hard-won redemption and high-stakes struggles.   🎵 Music: As 2026 draws to a close, NPR's All Songs Considered revisits some great songs from earlier in the year that might have been missed, including Northern Iowa's pop artist Kinji and Mexican singer Silvana Estrada.   🎮 Gaming: Nintendo's Ocarina of Time remake secures its legacy in gaming, but despite its high production values, NPR's James Perkins Mastromarino says it left him feeling oddly bereft.   ❓ Quiz: The midterms are over, and while this week was politics-heavy, that's not all that happened. This quiz offers a great recap of the week's diverse events.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Somali school girls play football during lunch break at the Howlwadag Primary School in Howlwadag District, south of Mogadishu. on October, 5, 2016.
                
                    Mohamed Abdiwahab/AFP/via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mohamed Abdiwahab/AFP/via Getty Images
    

   
   New global data suggest only a small minority of kids and teens get at least one hour a day of exercise that breaks a sweat, as recommended by the World Health Organization.A new report finds that generational wealth is enabling a record number of first-time homebuyers to pay in cash, increasing the gap between buyers and those priced out. The median age of first-time buyers also remains at a record high of 40.Herbert Blomstedt, a Swedish conductor whose remarkably long career saw him lead many of the world's major orchestras, died this week at home. He was 99.   
   This newsletter was edited by Dorine Bethea.

title: A judge blocked construction of Trump's arch at the 11th hour. What's next?
description: Demonstrators stand at Memorial Circle t
body:
Demonstrators stand at Memorial Circle to protest President Trump's proposed arch on Thursday night as a federal panel heard hours of testimony from concerned citizens. It voted to approve the structure.
                
                    Tom Brenner/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/Getty Images
    

   
   A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately.    Just before midnight Friday, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order — finalized and made public minutes later — barring the government from any construction work for 14 days, granting a request filed days earlier by the governments of D.C. and Virginia.   She laid out her reasoning in a 33-page opinion, in which she scrutinized the administration's competing justifications for the arch — particularly its sudden emphasis on national security — and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.   
   Trump administration officials have said work would take place 20 hours a day, year-round, for two to three years. In addition to questioning the arch's legality, D.C. and Virginia argue the construction would cause all sorts of financial and logistical disruptions.    "The threatened harms will materialize as soon as construction begins, in part because the traffic disruptions will occur immediately," Chutkan agreed.    Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after a federal planning commission packed with presidential allies granted final approval to the arch in an 8-4 vote. The National Capital Planning Commission heard nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure.   The Trump administration had previously told the court it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an expanding legal challenge.   A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.   Chutkan consolidated the lawsuits and asked the government to notify the court within an hour of commission approval, setting the stage for an 11th-hour ruling.    
   Thursday started with a protest on Memorial Circle, where dozens of people spoke against the arch. The grass underfoot was already marked with white paint. Lawyers for the government told the court in a midday filing that the lines were painted on Saturday by its designated construction firm, seemingly without authorization from the National Park Service.   The commission meeting began at 1 p.m. It was held virtually because of the high volume of public testimony: 131 people were signed up to speak.   Just minutes into public testimony, the livestream crashed, lengthening the meeting by about an hour until it was restored. Over the course of nearly nine hours, commissioners heard from dozens of veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and concerned citizens from D.C. and beyond.   Among their many concerns, critics said the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to the notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They have questions about its legality and its cost, which the administration has not confirmed.   Many see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital — and described Democrats' midterm sweep as a referendum against it.   
   "Leaving aside all of the legitimate concerns and challenges about the required approvals, funding, land use, single-source bidding, and peer review, the American people spoke this past Tuesday at the ballot box," said former D.C. resident Emi Yamauchi. "They said enough vanity projects, enough corruption, enough Reflecting Pool travesties."   Only a handful of speakers offered support for the arch, including Republican Reps. Andrew Clyde of Georgia and Brian Mast of Florida, both of whom are veterans.   
   Much of the night's testimony was heartfelt and personal: Many speakers had family members buried — or plans for their own future burials — at Arlington National Cemetery. Several implored the commissioners not to ruin their reputations by recording their support for the arch.   "[These are] warnings about the threat your own behavior poses to your political power, your moral authority, the legacy you leave to your descendants, and your eternal souls," said Stephen Eubank, some seven hours into the public testimony.   
   As the night wore on, a few speakers even questioned whether the commissioners — who were not shown on screen — were even listening. Many suggested the approval was a foregone conclusion, noting the political makeup of the commission and the fact that Trump-appointed Chair Mark Paoletta and several other members had expressed their support for the arch at the start of the meeting.   Deliberations began just before 10 p.m., and didn't last long.   
   The most vocal criticism came from D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson, a Democrat who sits on the commission. He asked questions about the arch's purpose and said that he was dissatisfied with the government's contradictory answers.   "We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plan," Mendelson said. He introduced a motion to postpone the vote until those plans could be submitted, or until the commission's next meeting in early December. The motion failed by a vote of 4 to 8.   Vice Chair Stuart Levenbach, a Trump appointee, said he was against delaying the vote because the "project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today," suggesting the government wanted to "commence building very quickly."   Within an hour, the commission had given the arch the green light and notified the judge accordingly. But any dreams of imminent construction were dashed by Friday — at least temporarily.   "While this decision prevents Donald Trump from immediately implementing his plans to create a monument to his own ego, the courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards to stop the Trump Administration from violating the law and proceeding with this project," Rep. Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said in a statement.   Trump-friendly commissioners downplayed legal concerns. The judge disagrees    During deliberations, Trump allies dismissed concerns that the arch would violate D.C.'s restrictions on building heights as well as federal environmental and historic preservation laws.   
   A core tenet of their legal argument is that Congress authorized the project in 1925, when it approved a pair of 166-foot columns on Memorial Circle that were never built.   "You're glorifying it by calling it an argument," Robert Weissman, the co-president of Public Citizen — the consumer rights nonprofit representing the veterans in their lawsuit — told NPR on Thursday. "To go back and look at a distinct and separate act of Congress a hundred years ago and say, 'Therefore, it authorizes the construction now,' is preposterous."   The administration maintains that the century-old authorization allows the arch to bypass modern requirements, like those of the 1986 Commemorative Works Act. It has increasingly painted the arch as an urgent matter of unfinished business, saying the 1925 act remains in effect because the grassy traffic circle is "incomplete."   
   That logic did not hold water with Chutkan.   "The sheer improbability that a 100-year-old statute would contain authority, unknown to every previous administration, to erect a 250-foot arch at a principal location in the Nation's capital indicates how far Defendants must stretch to justify this project," she wrote.   In recent days, administration officials have also leaned into the argument that the arch is necessary for national security.   Trump first announced on social media in September — 11 months after unveiling his proposal — that the structure would house snipers and ammunition, but specifics never followed. In a court filing last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described it as a "dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense."   
   At Thursday's meeting, however, administration officials struggled to elaborate beyond that seven-page filing, and ultimately confirmed that no national security analysis or details were included in the final plan. After considerable prompting from a skeptical Mendelson, Interior Department official Greg Wischer admitted that "specific national security functions have been filed under seal" in court, but the National Park Service "has not been privy to any national defense preparations."   Critics of the arch see this as another instance of Trump claiming national security to advance his own agenda, as in the case of the White House ballroom. The judge seemed skeptical, too.   
   "The court appreciates the government's significant interest in national security," Chutkan wrote. "But these recent and unsupported attestations of security aspects of a structure that has been extensively discussed over the last year appear nowhere in the planning documents on which the project was reviewed and approved."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A security camera watches over Memorial Circle on Thursday night.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   On Friday morning, the White House unveiled a website dedicated to what it's now calling the "Military Triumphal Arch."   The site plays a seemingly AI-generated video of the completed arch, topped with a burning eternal flame and entirely void of tourists and cars. (Mendelson's questions about traffic, including emergency response vehicles, did not get much airtime on Thursday). The website boasts the word "Triumph" in gold cursive, and describes the arch as "a solemn entrance to Arlington National Cemetery" — a disconnect that many critics have already noted in their public comments.   In a section called "An American Vision Finally Realized," the administration uses archival renderings to double down on its argument that the arch was authorized a century ago and has been sorely missing ever since.   "While such a grand monument was planned and dreamed of by all of America, it was a Dream that never got built because of the onset of the Great Depression of 1929 — But it will get built now," the website says.   Historic preservationists say Memorial Circle was left intentionally empty to preserve the symbolically significant view between the Lincoln Memorial and the former home of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee — one of dozens of historic sightlines that would be disrupted by a towering arch.   The website also provides some new, albeit vague, details about the arch's military capabilities. It says areas on the observation deck will be "set aside for snipers, countersnipers, and provisions for a sniper nest," and the base of the arch will be "designed for launching drones and other homeland security assets, if and when necessary."   
   "The Military component will play a large role in the planning and development of this Project," it reads. "It will be Highly Secretive but, at the same time, a Top Level and Lethal structure, the likes of which has not been seen in this Country before."   At a hearing last week, Chutkan questioned how the administration plans to reconcile the arch as both a military structure and a tourist attraction. Critics made that point throughout the day on Thursday, at the rally and the commission meeting.   "We are mightily perplexed by the assertion that this vainglorious arch will serve simultaneously as a gold-encrusted tourist attraction, outfitted with a gift shop and a viewing platform, and as a military fortification equipped with snipers, drones and live munitions," Susan Douglas of the activist group Third Act DMV said at the protest. "This is nothing more than the fever dream of a self-aggrandizing tyrant embellished by his sycophantic secretary of defense."   In a social media post Friday, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle slammed an "activist district court" for blocking construction and said, "We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."   Arch critics look to the courts and Congress for relief    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Protesters rallied under a miniature arch mockup at Memorial Circle on Thursday morning.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   Historic preservation groups wasted no time slamming both the process and the outcome of Thursday's commission vote.   Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, called the proceedings a "sham."   "It undermines the democratic process, violates federal statute, and insults our nation's veterans who have made the ultimate sacrifice," he said in a statement. "From the start, this Arch project has been driven by an artificial sense of urgency, while public opposition has been brushed aside."   Jimi Shaughnessy, veterans program manager for the National Parks Conservation Association, said in a statement that the organization is disappointed but not surprised. He vowed to "bring this to members of Congress, to ensure this arch is never built. Not here. Not ever."   
   Many Democratic lawmakers have vowed to stop — and investigate — the arch after they regain a Congressional majority in January.   Weissman said Congress doesn't need to act to stop the arch, since it never actively approved it. That decision, he said, will be up to the courts.   
   But, he added: "It would be fine if Congress takes additional measures to block construction, since we've seen this lawless administration circumvent the law and court orders so frequently."   Virginia Rep. Don Beyer has introduced a bill that would prohibit and defund the arch, and said Thursday he expects the number of co-sponsors to grow from 80 to at least 200 in the new year.   And Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, warned commissioners that companies and "officials working to advance a project not authorized by Congress will put themselves at legal risk."   He argued that the project violates federal environmental and historic preservation laws, which fall within the jurisdiction of the House committee he expects to soon lead.   "I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it, because, in case you hadn't heard, we'll soon have a new Congress that takes the rule of law very seriously," Huffman said.

schema.headline: A judge blocked construction of Trump's arch at the 11th hour. What's next?
